757.title: Isidore of Seville
757.hook: he tried to gather all human knowledge into one book
757.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Isidore of Seville and honors him as a Doctor of the Church; his Etymologies is still read by people who study how learning was kept and passed on.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregorian chant: the Church singing in unison. Your line was one voice.

What is a star? Why is a horse called a horse? What does a doctor do, what is a city, and how do you build a ship? One man in Spain set out to answer questions like these, and many more, in a single work. He wasn't a professor in a quiet library. He was a busy bishop in Seville, holding councils, teaching clergy. And still he kept writing, gathering what earlier writers knew about grammar, law, medicine, animals, stones, the stars and God, so it could sit on one shelf. Today, Isidore of Seville.
screen: `WHAT IS A STAR?` → `A BUSY BISHOP IN SEVILLE.` → `EVERYTHING ON ONE SHELF.`

segments.voice: His big work is called the Etymologies, and the title gives away his method: understand where a thing's name comes from, and you'll understand the thing faster. So he goes word by word. Here is the name, here is where it comes from, here is what it means. From there he opens out into everything: how to write, how to argue, how the body works, which trees grow where, what the Church's feasts mean. Isidore didn't claim to invent any of this. He collected it, reading the older writers, pagan and Christian, and pulling their work together so that what lay scattered could be found in one place. Not all of it holds up. Some of his word origins are guesses, and readers today smile at them. That doesn't take away what he was doing: keeping a whole world of learning within reach of one reader. One line from another of his books still gets passed around. Isidore wrote, roughly, that when we pray, we speak to God, and when we read, God speaks to us. For him, reading was never just collecting facts. It was half of a conversation. Catholics honor him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. His ambition was all knowledge. Not because one book could ever hold it, but because learning belonged inside a life turned toward God.
screen: `A BOOK OF NAMES AND THINGS.` · `GATHERED, NOT INVENTED.` · `SOME GUESSES, STILL A GIFT.` · then, large: `WHEN WE READ, GOD SPEAKS.` · then: `LEARNING INSIDE A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Pick an ordinary thing near you, a plant, a cup, the weather outside, your own breath, and look at it slowly, the way Isidore looked at a word. What is it made of, where did it come from, who made it or grew it? Let one question stay with you to look up later, and if you pray, thank God for one thing you'll understand a little better today.
Isidore. A bishop in Spain who gathered what earlier writers knew into one great book of names and things, so it wouldn't be lost. Today's word.
Your line: all knowledge. Tomorrow, a monk who wouldn't leave a sentence unfinished. That's day seven hundred fifty-seven.

758.title: Bede (d. 735)
758.hook: the historian of England finished translating John as he died
758.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Bede the Venerable and honors him as a Doctor of the Church; his history of the English Church is still read, and Cuthbert's letter about his death is often read alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isidore, the bishop who gathered the world's learning into one book. Your line was all knowledge.

A monastery in the north of England, in spring. An old monk is very sick and short of breath, and everyone around him can tell he's dying. He keeps working anyway: teaching, singing psalms, dictating to a young scribe, because there's a book he wants to finish. On the last day, the boy says there's still one sentence left to write. The old monk says, write it quickly. That monk, who wouldn't leave the sentence unfinished, is Bede.
screen: `A MONK IN THE NORTH OF ENGLAND.` → `TOO SICK, STILL WORKING.` → `ONE SENTENCE LEFT.`

segments.voice: Bede spent his life as a monk, praying the hours and writing: about the Bible, about time and the calendar, and above all a history of the Church among the English. That book is why he's remembered as a historian, and a careful one; he often tells you where a story came from and who told it to him. The story of his death comes from one of his students, a monk named Cuthbert, who wrote it down in a letter. In his last days, Cuthbert says, Bede was putting the Gospel of John into English, for the good of the Church, and working on other passages, dictating even as his breath failed. On the final day the young scribe, Wilbert, said, there is still one sentence not written down. Bede told him to write it. A little later the boy said, now it is written. And Bede answered, you've spoken truly, it is finished. Then, Cuthbert says, he asked to be held so he could face the place where he used to pray, and he died singing the Glory Be. A few days ago, Columba laid down his pen and left the next verse to the one who came after him. Bede did the opposite. And it is finished are the words John's Gospel gives Jesus on the cross; in the Douay-Rheims, "It is consummated." Some readers hear Bede's last words as a quiet echo of them. Catholics honor him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and call him the Venerable Bede. His gift is finishing. Not finishing everything. Finishing the next sentence.

759.title: Boniface and the oak
759.hook: an English monk fells a sacred oak in Germany and the mission grows; he's martyred in 754
759.tomorrow: John of Damascus and the icons
759.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Boniface, bishop and martyr, and churches in Germany are dedicated to him; the oak of Geismar is told as part of his story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bede, who kept dictating until the last sentence was written. Your line was finishing.

A huge old oak stands at a place called Geismar, in the land of Hesse. People gather there and honor the tree as holy, the dwelling of a god. One day a bishop from England, a monk by training, walks up to it with an axe, while a crowd watches and, the story says, curses him under its breath. He begins to cut. The question hangs in the air: if this tree belongs to a god, what happens to the man who strikes it? Today, Boniface and the oak.
screen: `AN OAK AT GEISMAR.` → `A MONK WITH AN AXE.` → `A CROWD WAITING.`

segments.voice: Our account comes from Willibald, a priest who wrote the life of Boniface from what his companions told him. Boniface was born in England, became a monk, and chose to leave home to preach among the peoples east of the Rhine; by the time of the oak, Willibald says, the pope had made him a bishop. Some people in Hesse, Willibald says, had been baptized but still honored the old sacred places, and one of those was a great oak. Boniface and his companions began to cut it down. After only a little cutting, a great wind shook the tree, and it crashed to the ground and broke into four pieces. The people who had cursed him stopped cursing and began to bless God. Boniface used the timber to build a small chapel, dedicated to Saint Peter. The wood of the old worship became the walls of the new. Willibald tells this as a victory, and that is how the story has been handed down. Some readers today also feel the loss: a tree people loved, cut down in front of them. Both can be held. It's a story of one man's courage, and of a people's old faith giving way. His mission grew; he organized churches and monasteries in Germany. Years later, Willibald says, in Frisia, he was killed by attackers while waiting to confirm new Christians, and he told his companions not to fight back. Catholics honor him as a saint and martyr. And the moment the crowd stopped breathing: the oak fell.

segments.voice: In the Bible's language, an idol is something given more trust than it can bear: a phone checked every few minutes, a number in a bank account, someone's approval. Breathe, and ask yourself gently what has grown too tall in your life; don't cut it down in anger, just name it and notice the hold it has. If you pray, hand that hold to God for these two minutes.

Your line: the oak fell. Courage and loss, both inside one story. Day seven hundred fifty-nine, done.

760.title: John of Damascus and the icons
760.hook: he defends images: God became visible, so he can be pictured
760.howItsDone: In Catholic and Orthodox churches people light candles before icons, bow, or kiss them, honoring the person shown; the Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint John Damascene as a Doctor of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boniface and the oak at Geismar. Your line was the oak fell.

A story is told of soldiers on a ladder at a palace gate, pulling down a picture of Christ. Across an empire, painted images are being taken out of churches, plastered over, broken; the emperor's party says pictures of holy things are idols, and must go. Far away, in a monastery near Jerusalem, outside the emperor's reach, a monk named John, from a family that served in Damascus, picks up his pen to argue for the pictures. His argument doesn't start with art. It starts with Christmas. Today's word is icon.
screen: `PICTURES PULLED DOWN.` → `A MONK OUTSIDE THE EMPIRE.` → `IT STARTS WITH CHRISTMAS.`

segments.voice: Icon comes from the Greek word for image, eikon. The letter to the Colossians uses it about Christ himself; in the Douay-Rheims it calls him "the image of the invisible God." That's John's starting point. In the old law, God gave no shape to look at, so nobody could paint him. But now, John says, God has been seen. He was born, he had a face, he ate and walked and was touched. So a painter of Christ isn't inventing the invisible God out of his own head. He's painting what people saw. John's best-known line runs, roughly: I do not worship matter; I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake, and through matter worked my salvation. Wood, paint, bread, water, a body: God used stuff, so stuff can be honored. Then a careful distinction. Worship belongs to God alone. An icon receives honor, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love, and, borrowing a line from Basil the Great, John says the honor passes through the picture to the person it shows. Later, a council of bishops at Nicaea agreed and approved the honoring of images. Catholics and Orthodox Christians both honor John as a saint, and Catholics call him a Doctor of the Church. Some people describe an icon this way: a window, not a wall. Something to look through, not to stop at.

segments.voice: If you have an icon or a holy card nearby, use it; if not, glance at one on a screen, then set the screen face down and hold the image in your mind. Look first at the eyes, then the hands, and let your gaze rest without analyzing, breathing slowly. If you pray, let the image carry your prayer past it.
Icon. From the Greek for image: a holy picture that, for those who honor it, points past itself to the one it shows. Today's word.
Your line: a window, not a wall. A picture can point past itself. Until tomorrow.

761.title: The Holy Mountain
761.hook: Mount Athos, Orthodox monks praying since the tenth century
761.carry: the garden of the Mother of God
761.howItsDone: Orthodox monks on Mount Athos keep long night services and pray the Jesus Prayer through the day; Catholics who visit come as pilgrims and guests, and Catholics pray for unity with the Orthodox churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of Damascus and the word icon. Your line was a window, not a wall.

Pilgrims come by boat. A long finger of land in northern Greece runs out into the sea, rising to a peak, and along its cliffs and wooded slopes stand monasteries, some of them hanging over the water. Before dawn a wooden board is struck with a mallet, and monks walk to church in the dark, morning after morning. The Orthodox call it simply the Holy Mountain. Today, Mount Athos.
screen: `A FINGER OF LAND IN THE SEA.` → `A BOARD STRUCK BEFORE DAWN.` → `MONKS WALK TO CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Athos is a peninsula given over to monastic life. It belongs to Greece, but the monasteries govern much of their own life on it. Only men may visit, a rule the monks keep as part of their tradition. Orthodox tradition calls Athos the garden of the Mother of God, and a story says Mary herself came ashore there and blessed it. The center of the monks' day is the long services of the church, often through the night, and between them, work and silence. Again and again they pray a short prayer called the Jesus Prayer, asking Jesus, the Son of God, for mercy. It grows out of the Gospels. In Luke, a tax collector stands at the back of the Temple, won't even lift his eyes, and says, in the Douay-Rheims, "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." The monks of Athos have turned a cry like that into a way of breathing. Why does a Catholic lesson go there? The Orthodox and the Catholic Church share the apostles, the sacraments, the early councils and the Fathers you've been meeting, but they've been apart a long time and are not in full communion. Catholic teaching calls the Orthodox churches sister churches, and honors their monks' prayer as a treasure of the whole Church. Some Catholics make the journey to Athos as pilgrims, as guests of the Orthodox. For the monks, the holy mountain is about Mary's blessing and the prayer kept there, not the rock.

segments.voice: Slow your breath and picture a monk somewhere right now, standing in a dim church or walking a path above the sea, praying for the world, which includes you. If you pray, carry the tax collector's words from Luke on your breath: O God, be merciful to me a sinner. If you don't, just keep company with them in silence.

Your line: the garden of the Mother of God. Far away, before dawn, the prayer goes on. That's seven hundred sixty-one days.

762.title: Cyril and Methodius (9th century)
762.hook: brothers who made an alphabet so Slavs could pray in their own tongue
762.howItsDone: Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep a feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, and some Slavic churches, Catholic and Orthodox, still celebrate the liturgy in Church Slavonic, the language the brothers wrote down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mount Athos, where monks pray for the world before dawn. Your line was the garden of the Mother of God.
screen: `THE GARDEN OF THE MOTHER OF GOD.`

segments.voice: A message arrives in Constantinople from a Slavic prince far to the north. His people have heard Christian preachers, he says, but in languages they don't understand. Send us a teacher who can explain the faith in our own words. The emperor turns to two brothers from Thessalonica who grew up hearing Slavic spoken around them: one a scholar, the other an experienced administrator turned monk. There's one problem. The Slavs have no letters, and you can't hand someone a Gospel in a language nobody has ever written down. Today, Cyril and Methodius.
screen: `A PRINCE ASKS FOR A TEACHER.` → `TWO BROTHERS FROM THESSALONICA.` → `A LANGUAGE WITH NO LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Our account is the old Slavonic life of the younger brother, who was called Constantine; he took the name Cyril only near the end, as a monk. When the request came, the life says, Constantine prayed, and God showed him the letters. He made an alphabet and began to translate, and the first words he wrote were the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God." The brothers went north and taught in the Slavic language. They translated the Gospels and the prayers of the liturgy, so people could hear the Mass in their own speech. Not everyone liked it. Some clergy, the life says, argued that God could be praised only in three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Constantine answered with verse after verse of scripture. One psalm, in the Douay-Rheims, says, "Let every spirit praise the Lord." Every spirit, not three languages. The brothers traveled to the pope, who welcomed them and blessed their Slavonic books. Cyril died in Rome. Methodius went back north as a bishop, and through hard years the work went on, after he was gone, in the hands of their students. Catholic and Orthodox Christians both honor the two as saints, and John Paul the Second named them patrons of Europe, together with Benedict. For the brothers, the Gospel was meant to reach people in the words they already spoke.
screen: `GOD SHOWED HIM THE LETTERS.` · `IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.` · `NOT ONLY THREE LANGUAGES.` · `BLESSED IN ROME.` · then, large: `IN THEIR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone near you whose first language isn't yours, a neighbor, a coworker, a grandparent, and a word they'd love to hear from you: hello, thank you, peace. Breathe slowly and say it quietly a few times, getting the sounds right, standing for a moment inside another tongue. If you pray, thank God for the language you first prayed in, or first heard love in.
Cyril. The monk, born Constantine, who made an alphabet for the Slavs and translated the Gospels with his brother Methodius. Today's word.
Your line: in their own tongue. A whole alphabet, made so a people could hear. See you tomorrow.

763.title: Charlemagne (800)
763.hook: crowned in Rome on Christmas Day; schools and a mixed legacy
763.howItsDone: Charlemagne is not a saint on the Church's universal calendar; his schools and the books copied in his time are studied as part of how the Church kept learning alive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril and Methodius, who gave the Slavs letters. Your line was in their own tongue.

Christmas, in Saint Peter's in Rome. The king of the Franks has come to Mass: tall, his biographer tells us, and usually dressed plainly, in the clothes of his own people. As he rises from prayer, the pope places a crown on his head, and the crowd acclaims him as emperor. His biographer, Einhard, adds something odd. Charles said afterward that if he'd known what the pope intended, he wouldn't have gone into the church that day, feast or no feast. Today, Charlemagne.
screen: `CHRISTMAS IN SAINT PETER'S.` → `A CROWN AFTER PRAYER.` → `I WOULDN'T HAVE COME.`

segments.voice: Nobody is sure what Charles meant. Some readers think he didn't want the pope deciding who was emperor; others think it was modesty for show. Einhard doesn't explain. Take the cathedrals side first. Charles cared about learning. He gathered scholars at his court, among them Alcuin, a teacher from York. He wanted priests who could read, schools attached to monasteries and cathedrals, and books copied clearly. Einhard says Charles himself tried to learn to write late in life, keeping tablets under his pillow, but began too late to get far. Now the crowns side. Charles was also a conqueror. Einhard describes long wars against the Saxons, who were made to give up their old worship and accept baptism as a condition of peace. Baptism under a sword. Even in his own court, voices pushed back: Alcuin wrote that faith comes from the will and can't be forced, that a person can be drawn to faith but not compelled into it. So which is he, a builder or a conqueror? Honestly, both. Einhard records the schools and the books, and he records the Saxons too. That closes a week of people who carried the faith in very different ways: Isidore gathering all knowledge, Bede finishing, Boniface's oak falling, John of Damascus's window, the monks on Mount Athos, two brothers teaching in their own tongue, and today a crown, with a cathedral school beside it.
screen: `A CROWN HE DIDN'T EXPECT.` · `SCHOOLS AND CLEAR BOOKS.` · `BAPTISM UNDER A SWORD.` · `FAITH CAN'T BE FORCED.` · then, large: `CROWNS AND CATHEDRALS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small place where you have power over someone: a child, a team at work, a younger sibling, even a pet. Ask slowly where you've used that power to build something good, like a school, and where you've used it to push someone into your way of doing things, and look at both without judgment. If you pray, ask God for the grace to draw people, never to force them.
